questions.problem:
Consider the function $f$ defined by $f(x)=\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}.$

Current part:

Calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${f}^{′}(x)\,=\,$ 

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=7$ and $v(x)=2{x}^{2}-5x-3,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=0,\,{v}^{′}(x)=4x-5.
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x){v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(0)\cdot (2{x}^{2}-5x-3)-7\cdot (4x-5)}{{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-7\cdot (4x-5)}{{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{7(5-4x)}{{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

The slope of the tangent line to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at $x=2$ is

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}

questions.worked_solution:
The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(2).$ In part 1, we found

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{7(5-4x)}{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=2,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{7(5-4\cdot 2)}{(2\cdot {2}^{2}-5\cdot 2-3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot (-3)}{(-5)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{21}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line to the curve at $x=2$ is $-\frac{21}{25}.$

questions.worked_solution:
In part 2 we found that ${f}^{′}(2)=-\frac{21}{25}.$ Also,

$$
f(2)=\frac{7}{2\cdot {2}^{2}-5\cdot 2-3}=-\frac{7}{5}.
$$

The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=5-25f(x)$ and $v=g(x)+3.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-25{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-25{f}^{′}(x)\cdot (g(x)+3)-(5-25f(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x)+3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=2,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & =\frac{-25{f}^{′}(2)\cdot (g(2)+3)-(5-25f(2))\cdot {g}^{′}(2)}{(g(2)+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-25\cdot (-\frac{21}{25})\cdot (-2+3)-(5-25\cdot (-\frac{7}{5}))\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{(-2+3)^{2}} \\  & =21-20 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

At which values of $x\in (-\frac{1}{2},3)$ does $f$ have a critical point?

questions.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

In part 1, we obtained

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{7(5-4x)}{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)^{2}}.
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

* First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7(5-4x)}{(2{x}^{2}-5x-3)^{2}} & =0 \\ 7(5-4x) & =0 \\ 5-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has a stationary point at $x=\frac{5}{4}.$

* Second, we find the points in the domain of $f(x)$ where ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. Factoring our expression for ${f}^{′}(x),$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{7(5-4x)}{[(2x+1)(x-3)]^{2}}.
$$

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist at $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=3.$ But these points do not lie in the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},3).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the only critical point of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{5}{4}.$

$$

and the critical point $x=\frac{5}{4}.$ We use the first derivative test to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum.

Let's choose the test points $x=0,2$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{7(4\cdot 0-5)}{(2\cdot {0}^{2}-5\cdot 0-3)^{2}}=\frac{35}{9}>0 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{7(4\cdot 2-5)}{(2\cdot {2}^{2}-5\cdot 2-3)^{2}}=-\frac{21}{25}<0\end{aligned}

| $f$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

* At $x=\frac{5}{4},$ the first derivative changes sign from positive to negative. Therefore, $x=\frac{5}{4}$ is a local maximum.

Current part:

Given that

$$
{\int }_{4}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=A{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}+B{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants, find $A$ and $B.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $A=$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator of $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)=\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}=\frac{7}{(x-3)(2x+1)}
$$

Our task is to find $A$ and $B$ such that

$$
\frac{7}{(x-3)(2x+1)}=\frac{A}{x-3}+\frac{B}{2x+1}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x-3)(2x+1)$ gives

$$
7=A(2x+1)+B(x-3).
$$

Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+1)+B(-\frac{1}{2}-3) \\ 7 & =-\frac{7}{2}B \\ B & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(2\cdot 3+1)+B(3-3) \\ 7 & =7A \\ A & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{7}{(x-3)(2x+1)}=\frac{1}{x-3}-\frac{2}{2x+1}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{x-3}-\frac{2}{2x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}-2{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A=1$ and $B=-2.$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}-2{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's calculate the indefinite integral first. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}-2\int \frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-3}{2x+1}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the improper integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-3}{2x+1}|]}_{4}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{a-3}{2a+1}|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{9}|) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1-\frac{3}{a}}{2+\frac{1}{a}}|)-\operatorname{ln}⁡{9}^{-1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡9 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
